name: Roman conquest of Italy
summary: Over about 125 years Rome went from a city sacked by Gauls to the master of the Italian peninsula south of the Po. It beat the Latins, the Samnites and their Etruscan and Gallic allies, and finally the Greek cities of the south and their champion Pyrrhus of Epirus. Rome bound the defeated to it as allies who supplied soldiers, the manpower that would carry it through the wars with Carthage.

steps.label: c. 390 BC
steps.title: The Gauls sack Rome
steps.text: Rome had just taken its Etruscan rival Veii when a Gallic war band of the Senones under Brennus came south from the Po valley. It routed the Roman army at the Allia river, eleven miles from the city, and sacked Rome, leaving only after it was paid in gold. The disaster pushed Rome to build stronger walls and reorganise its army.

events.name: Battle of the Allia
events.text: The Gauls broke the Roman army in a single charge north of the city.

events.name: Gallic sack of Rome
events.text: The Gauls plundered Rome and left only after being paid a ransom in gold.

steps.label: 343 to 338 BC
steps.title: Campania and the Latin War
steps.text: Rome answered a call from Capua and fought the Samnites of the Apennines for the rich plain of Campania in the First Samnite War. Its Latin allies then rose against Roman dominance, and the consul Manlius Torquatus crushed them. In the settlement of 338 BC Rome dissolved the Latin League and bound each city to itself, the model for its whole system of Italian alliances.

events.name: Battle of Mount Gaurus
events.text: Rome's first victory over the Samnites secured Capua.

events.name: Battle of Trifanum
events.text: Manlius Torquatus broke the Latin revolt.

events.name: Latin settlement
events.text: Rome dissolved the Latin League and tied each city to itself by separate treaty.

steps.label: 326 to 304 BC
steps.title: The Caudine Forks
steps.text: The Second Samnite War was a struggle for central Italy. In 321 BC the Samnite general Gavius Pontius trapped a whole Roman army in the pass of the Caudine Forks and sent it under the yoke. Rome recovered, built the Via Appia toward Campania, allied with the Apulians behind the Samnites and won at Bovianum in 305 BC.

events.name: Caudine Forks
events.text: A Roman army surrendered in a mountain pass and was sent home in disgrace.

events.name: Battle of Bovianum
events.text: Rome took the Samnite capital and forced peace the next year.

steps.label: 298 to 290 BC
steps.title: Sentinum
steps.text: In the Third Samnite War the Samnite leader Gellius Egnatius marched north to join Gauls, Etruscans and Umbrians in a grand coalition against Rome. At Sentinum Fabius Rullianus and Decius Mus, who sacrificed himself in the battle, destroyed the combined army. The Samnites submitted in 290 BC and Rome annexed the Sabine country, cutting Italy in two from sea to sea.

events.name: Battle of Sentinum
events.text: The largest battle yet fought in Italy broke the Samnite, Gallic and Etruscan alliance.

events.name: Samnites submit
events.text: The Samnites accepted alliance on Roman terms.

steps.label: 280 to 279 BC
steps.title: Pyrrhus lands in Italy
steps.text: Tarentum, the richest Greek city in Italy, called in King Pyrrhus of Epirus with a professional army and war elephants. Pyrrhus beat the Romans at Heraclea and Asculum and marched within forty miles of Rome, but his losses were so heavy that a costly win is still called a Pyrrhic victory. Rome refused to negotiate while he stood in Italy.

events.name: Battle of Heraclea
events.text: Pyrrhus' phalanx and elephants beat Rome's legions in their first meeting.

events.name: Battle of Asculum
events.text: Another win at a ruinous cost, the original Pyrrhic victory.

steps.label: 275 to 264 BC
steps.title: Beneventum and the fall of Tarentum
steps.text: Pyrrhus spent three years fighting Carthage in Sicily, then returned to Italy and was checked at Beneventum by Manius Curius Dentatus. He sailed home, Tarentum surrendered in 272 BC, and by 264 BC Rome controlled all of Italy south of the Po. That year a call for help from Messana across the strait drew Rome into Sicily and the First Punic War.

events.name: Battle of Beneventum
events.text: Pyrrhus failed to break the Romans and gave up on Italy.

events.name: Fall of Tarentum
events.text: The last great Greek city of the south became a Roman ally.

events.name: Messana appeals to Rome
events.text: Rome's answer led straight into war with Carthage.

name: Punic Wars
summary: Rome and Carthage fought three wars over 118 years for control of the western Mediterranean. Rome won Sicily at sea in the first, survived Hannibal's invasion of Italy across the Alps to win the second at Zama, and destroyed Carthage itself in the third. Victory made Rome the dominant power of the Mediterranean world.

steps.label: 264 to 260 BC
steps.title: First Punic War: the fight for Sicily
steps.text: A dispute over Messana drew Appius Claudius across the strait into Sicily, the first time Roman legions fought outside Italy. Rome won Syracuse over to its side and took the Carthaginian base of Agrigentum, then built its first real war fleet and beat Carthage at sea off Mylae with the corvus boarding bridge.

events.name: Siege of Agrigentum
events.text: Rome took and sacked Carthage's main base in southern Sicily.

events.name: Battle of Mylae
events.text: Rome's first great naval victory, won by boarding Carthaginian ships.

steps.label: 256 to 255 BC
steps.title: Invasion of Africa
steps.text: Rome sent a huge fleet south, smashed the Carthaginian navy off Cape Ecnomus and landed an army under Regulus near Carthage. Carthage hired the Spartan general Xanthippus, whose elephants and cavalry destroyed Regulus' army near Tunis, and storms then wrecked the Roman fleet on the way home.

events.name: Battle of Cape Ecnomus
events.text: One of the largest naval battles of antiquity opened the way to Africa.

events.name: Battle of Tunis
events.text: Xanthippus destroyed Regulus' army and captured him.

steps.label: 249 to 241 BC
steps.title: Aegates Islands
steps.text: The war ground on around the Carthaginian strongholds of western Sicily, where Hamilcar Barca held out on Mount Eryx. Rome lost a fleet at Drepana, but a new fleet paid for by private citizens under Lutatius Catulus destroyed Carthage's relief convoy off the Aegates Islands. Carthage gave up Sicily and paid a heavy indemnity.

fronts.label: Siege lines at Lilybaeum and Drepana

events.name: Battle of Drepana
events.text: Adherbal destroyed most of the Roman fleet attacking Drepana.

events.name: Battle of the Aegates
events.text: Rome's decisive naval victory ended the First Punic War.

events.name: Treaty of Lutatius
events.text: Carthage evacuated Sicily, which became Rome's first province.

steps.label: 219 to 218 BC
steps.title: Hannibal crosses the Alps
steps.text: After losing Sicily, Hamilcar Barca built a new Carthaginian empire in Spain. His son Hannibal took Saguntum, Rome declared war, and in 218 BC Hannibal marched from New Carthage over the Pyrenees, the Rhone and the Alps with an army and war elephants. He arrived in the Po valley with about 26,000 men, raised the Gauls and beat the Roman armies at the Ticinus and the Trebia.

events.name: Siege of Saguntum
events.text: Hannibal's capture of Rome's Spanish ally started the war.

events.name: Battle of the Ticinus
events.text: Hannibal's cavalry routed Publius Scipio's army, wounding the consul.

events.name: Battle of the Trebia
events.text: Hannibal ambushed and destroyed the combined consular armies.

steps.label: 217 to 216 BC
steps.title: Trasimene and Cannae
steps.text: Hannibal crossed the Apennines and trapped a Roman army on the shore of Lake Trasimene. Fabius Maximus then shadowed him without giving battle, but in 216 BC Rome sought a decision and at Cannae Hannibal's double envelopment annihilated the largest army it had ever fielded. Capua and much of southern Italy went over to Carthage, yet Rome refused to make peace.

events.name: Battle of Lake Trasimene
events.text: Hannibal ambushed a consular army in the lakeside fog and destroyed it.

events.name: Battle of Cannae
events.text: Hannibal's double envelopment killed perhaps 50,000 Romans in one day.

events.name: Capua defects
events.text: Italy's second city went over to Hannibal.

steps.label: 211 to 206 BC
steps.title: Rome strikes back
steps.text: Rome wore Hannibal down in Italy, retaking Capua and Tarentum, while Publius Cornelius Scipio took the war to Spain and stormed New Carthage. Hasdrubal Barca slipped out of Spain to reinforce his brother, but the consul Claudius Nero marched north from Apulia and destroyed him at the Metaurus. Scipio's victory at Ilipa in 206 BC drove Carthage out of Spain.

fronts.label: Hannibal confined to the south, 207 BC

moves.label: Scipio to New Carthage and Ilipa

events.name: Capture of New Carthage
events.text: Scipio stormed Carthage's capital in Spain in a single day.

events.name: Battle of the Metaurus
events.text: Hasdrubal's army was destroyed before it could join Hannibal.

events.name: Battle of Ilipa
events.text: Scipio's victory ended Carthaginian power in Spain.

steps.label: 204 to 201 BC
steps.title: Zama
steps.text: Scipio landed in Africa near Utica and, with the Numidian prince Masinissa as an ally, beat Carthage's armies in the field. Carthage recalled Hannibal from Italy after fifteen years, and at Zama Scipio defeated him in the war's final battle. The peace of 201 BC stripped Carthage of its fleet and its empire.

events.name: Battle of Zama
events.text: Scipio and Masinissa defeated Hannibal and ended the Second Punic War.

events.name: Peace of 201 BC
events.text: Carthage gave up Spain and its fleet and paid tribute for fifty years.

steps.label: 149 to 146 BC
steps.title: Third Punic War: Carthage destroyed
steps.text: Rome, urged on by Cato, used a Carthaginian war with Masinissa's Numidia as a pretext to send an army to Africa. Carthage handed over its weapons but refused to abandon its city, and held out for three years. Scipio Aemilianus stormed it in 146 BC, razed it and made its territory the Roman province of Africa.

events.name: Siege of Carthage
events.text: Scipio Aemilianus took the city street by street and razed it.

events.name: Province of Africa
events.text: Carthage's land became a Roman province governed from Utica.

name: Roman conquest of Hispania
summary: Rome came to Spain in 218 BC to fight Carthage and stayed for two centuries of war against the peoples of the interior. Lusitanians under Viriathus, Celtiberians at Numantia, the rebel Roman Sertorius and finally the mountain Cantabrians and Astures resisted in turn until Augustus and Agrippa finished the conquest in 19 BC. Hispania became one of the most Romanised parts of the empire, the root of the Latin languages of Iberia.

steps.label: 218 to 206 BC
steps.title: Rome arrives to fight Carthage
steps.text: While Hannibal marched on Italy, Gnaeus Scipio landed at Emporion and held the line of the Ebro. Both Scipio brothers were killed in 211 BC, but the younger Publius Scipio stormed New Carthage in 209 BC and drove the Carthaginians out of Spain after Ilipa in 206 BC. Rome kept the conquered east and south coasts.

events.name: Battle of Cissa
events.text: Gnaeus Scipio won Rome's first foothold north of the Ebro.

events.name: Capture of New Carthage
events.text: Scipio seized Carthage's capital, arsenal and treasury in Spain.

events.name: Battle of Ilipa
events.text: Carthage's last army in Spain was destroyed.

steps.label: 197 to 179 BC
steps.title: Two provinces and the first revolts
steps.text: In 197 BC Rome organised its gains as Hither and Further Spain, and the tribes rose almost at once against tribute and governors. Cato the Elder crushed the northeast in 195 BC, and Tiberius Gracchus pushed into Celtiberia and in 179 BC made treaties that kept the peace for a generation. The interior and the west remained free.

fronts.label: Edge of Roman control, c. 180 BC

events.name: Cato at Emporion
events.text: Cato defeated the rebel tribes of the northeast.

events.name: Treaties of Gracchus
events.text: Fair terms for the Celtiberians brought twenty-five years of peace.

steps.label: 155 to 139 BC
steps.title: Viriathus and the Lusitanians
steps.text: The Lusitanians of the far west raided the Roman south, and in 150 BC the governor Galba massacred thousands who had surrendered. A survivor, the shepherd Viriathus, led eight years of guerrilla war from the hills, beating army after army until Rome recognised him as a friend of the Roman people in 140 BC. The next year Rome bribed his companions to murder him.

events.name: Galba's massacre
events.text: The slaughter of surrendered Lusitanians turned a raid war into a national revolt.

events.name: Murder of Viriathus
events.text: Bribed by Rome, his own envoys killed him in his sleep.

steps.label: 143 to 133 BC
steps.title: Numantia
steps.text: The Celtiberian hill town of Numantia defied Rome for ten years and humiliated several consuls. In 134 BC Scipio Aemilianus, destroyer of Carthage, arrived, restored discipline and surrounded the town with a ring of walls and camps. After fifteen months of starvation Numantia surrendered and was razed, breaking the resistance of the central plateau.

events.name: Siege of Numantia
events.text: The starved defenders surrendered and the town was destroyed.

steps.label: 80 to 72 BC
steps.title: Sertorius
steps.text: Quintus Sertorius, a Roman general on the losing side of Rome's civil war, made Spain his base and won the Lusitanians and Celtiberians to his cause. For years he beat the Senate's armies under Metellus Pius and the young Pompey with hit and run warfare. In 72 BC his own officer Perperna murdered him, and Pompey quickly mopped up.

fronts.label: Line of the Sertorian war, 76 BC

events.name: Battle of the Sucro
events.text: Sertorius mauled Pompey before Metellus arrived to save him.

events.name: Murder of Sertorius
events.text: Killed at a banquet in Osca, his capital, by his officer Perperna.

steps.label: 29 to 19 BC
steps.title: The Cantabrian Wars
steps.text: Only the mountain north still held out. Augustus came in person in 26 BC and sent three columns from Segisama into the Cantabrian mountains, while his legates fought the Astures around Lancia. Revolts flared again and again until Agrippa finished the conquest in 19 BC, two hundred years after the Romans first landed.

events.name: Fall of Lancia
events.text: The stronghold of the Astures surrendered to Carisius.

events.name: Agrippa ends the war
events.text: The last Cantabrian rising was crushed and Hispania was fully Roman.

name: Maccabean Revolt
summary: Jewish rebels led by the priest Mattathias and his sons, the Maccabees, rose against the Seleucid king Antiochus IV after he outlawed Jewish worship and defiled the Temple. Judah Maccabee's guerrilla army beat several Seleucid forces, retook Jerusalem and rededicated the Temple in 164 BC, the origin of Hanukkah. Judah fell in 160 BC, but his brothers went on to found the independent Hasmonean kingdom.

steps.label: 167 to 166 BC
steps.title: Revolt at Modiin
steps.text: Antiochus IV banned the Jewish law and set up a pagan altar in the Temple of Jerusalem. In the village of Modiin the priest Mattathias killed a royal officer and a Jew who sacrificed, then fled to the hills with his five sons. His son Judah, called Maccabee, the hammer, took over the band and ambushed the Seleucid columns sent against it.

events.name: Mattathias rises
events.text: The killing at Modiin began the revolt.

events.name: Battle of Beth Horon
events.text: Judah ambushed Seron's column in the steep pass.

steps.label: 165 to 164 BC
steps.title: Emmaus and the Temple
steps.text: The regent Lysias sent a large army under Gorgias and Nicanor, but Judah surprised their camp at Emmaus. Lysias came himself by the southern road and was beaten at Beth Zur. Judah entered Jerusalem, cleansed the Temple and rededicated it in December 164 BC, the festival of Hanukkah.

events.name: Battle of Emmaus
events.text: Judah's night march caught the Seleucid army divided.

events.name: Battle of Beth Zur
events.text: Lysias was turned back on the road from Idumea.

events.name: Rededication of the Temple
events.text: Judah purified the Temple and restored Jewish worship.

steps.label: 162 BC
steps.title: Beth Zechariah
steps.text: Lysias returned with the boy king Antiochus V, a far larger army and war elephants. He beat Judah at Beth Zechariah, where Judah's brother Eleazar died stabbing an elephant from beneath, and besieged the Temple mount. News of a rival regent at Antioch forced Lysias to make peace and withdraw, repealing the ban on Jewish religion.

events.name: Battle of Beth Zechariah
events.text: Seleucid phalanx and elephants defeated the Maccabees.

events.name: Peace of Lysias
events.text: The Seleucids restored religious freedom, the revolt's first aim.

steps.label: 161 to 160 BC
steps.title: Adasa and Elasa
steps.text: The war went on as a fight for power in Judea. Judah destroyed Nicanor's army at Adasa in 161 BC, but the next year the general Bacchides came with a fresh army and killed Judah at Elasa. His brother Jonathan carried on the struggle, and by 142 BC Simon, the last brother, ruled an independent Judea.

events.name: Battle of Adasa
events.text: Nicanor was killed and his army routed.

events.name: Battle of Elasa
events.text: Judah Maccabee fell fighting against Bacchides' larger army.

name: Han conquest of Nanyue and Gojoseon
summary: Emperor Wu of Han sent armies against the kingdoms on China's southern and northeastern edges. In 111 BC Han forces took Panyu and annexed Nanyue, bringing northern Vietnam under Chinese rule for about a thousand years, and in 108 BC they took Wanggeom and replaced Gojoseon with four commanderies in northern Korea. The wars fixed the outer limits of the Han world for centuries.

steps.label: 112 BC
steps.title: War on Nanyue
steps.text: Nanyue, a kingdom founded by a Qin general around Panyu, was moving toward submission to Han when its chancellor Lu Jia killed the pro-Han queen mother, the young king and the Han envoys. Emperor Wu sent several armies south over the Nanling passes, led by Lu Bode and Yang Pu, with others coming down the rivers.

events.name: Lu Jia's coup
events.text: The murder of the king and the Han envoys gave Emperor Wu his reason for war.

steps.label: 111 to 110 BC
steps.title: Fall of Panyu
steps.text: Yang Pu's troops reached Panyu first and set it on fire, and Lu Bode received the surrender of its defenders. Lu Jia and the king fled by sea and were captured. Nanyue became nine commanderies stretching down to Jiaozhi and Jiuzhen in the Red River and Ma River plains of Vietnam, and in 110 BC Han also conquered Minyue on the Fujian coast.

events.name: Fall of Panyu
events.text: The Nanyue capital was burned and the kingdom annexed.

events.name: Jiaozhi commandery
events.text: Northern Vietnam entered a thousand years of Chinese rule.

events.name: Conquest of Minyue
events.text: Han armies overran the last independent Yue kingdom on the coast.

steps.label: 109 BC
steps.title: Invasion of Gojoseon
steps.text: King Ugeo of Gojoseon blocked contact between Han and the states of southern Korea, and the killing of a Han envoy led to war. Yang Pu crossed the Bohai Sea from Shandong with a fleet while Xun Zhi marched overland from Liaodong. Both were beaten back at first, then closed on the capital Wanggeom.

events.name: Yang Pu repulsed
events.text: Gojoseon troops routed Yang Pu's landing force near the capital.

steps.label: 108 BC
steps.title: Four Commanderies
steps.text: Besieged and divided, Gojoseon's ministers murdered King Ugeo and the capital fell in the summer of 108 BC. Han divided the land into four commanderies, Lelang around Pyongyang, Zhenfan, Lintun and Xuantu. Lelang lasted until AD 313 and carried Chinese writing and goods into Korea and Japan.

events.name: Fall of Wanggeom
events.text: Gojoseon's capital surrendered after King Ugeo was killed by his ministers.

events.name: Lelang commandery
events.text: Han rule in northern Korea began, centred on Pyongyang.

name: Mithridatic Wars
summary: Mithridates VI of Pontus, the most dangerous enemy of the late Roman Republic, fought Rome three times for control of Anatolia and the Aegean. Sulla drove him out of Greece, Lucullus invaded Pontus and Armenia, and Pompey finally broke him in 66 BC and reorganised the whole East. The wars added Anatolia and Syria to the Roman world and made Pompey the greatest man in Rome.

steps.label: 89 to 88 BC
steps.title: The Asian Vespers
steps.text: Provoked by Rome's ally Bithynia, Mithridates swept through Roman Asia while Rome was distracted by war in Italy. He ordered the killing of every Roman and Italian in the province, perhaps 80,000 people, in a single day, then sent his general Archelaus across the Aegean, where Athens joined him.

events.name: Battle of the Amnias
events.text: Mithridates' generals destroyed the Bithynian army.

events.name: Asian Vespers
events.text: Romans and Italians across Asia were massacred on the king's order.

steps.label: 87 to 85 BC
steps.title: Sulla in Greece
steps.text: Sulla landed in Epirus with five legions, besieged Athens and the Piraeus, and stormed Athens in March 86 BC. He then smashed Archelaus' much larger armies at Chaeronea and Orchomenus in Boeotia. In a hurry to return to civil war in Rome, Sulla made peace at Dardanus: Mithridates gave up his conquests but kept his throne.

events.name: Siege of Athens
events.text: Sulla stormed the city and sacked it.

events.name: Battle of Chaeronea
events.text: Sulla's legions routed Archelaus' army.

events.name: Peace of Dardanus
events.text: Mithridates gave back all his conquests.

steps.label: 74 to 71 BC
steps.title: Third war: Cyzicus
steps.text: After a brief second war, the death of the king of Bithynia, who left his kingdom to Rome, set off the third and longest war. Mithridates invaded Bithynia and besieged Cyzicus, but Lucullus cut his supply lines and starved his army. Lucullus then invaded Pontus and won at Cabira, and Mithridates fled to his son-in-law Tigranes of Armenia.

moves.label: Lucullus relieves Cyzicus and invades Pontus

events.name: Siege of Cyzicus
events.text: Mithridates' great army melted away from hunger and disease.

events.name: Battle of Cabira
events.text: Lucullus broke the Pontic army in its homeland.

steps.label: 69 to 67 BC
steps.title: Tigranocerta
steps.text: Lucullus crossed the Euphrates and routed the huge army of Tigranes at his new capital Tigranocerta. But his march toward the Armenian heartland failed when his exhausted troops mutinied, and Mithridates slipped back into Pontus and destroyed a Roman army at Zela.

events.name: Battle of Tigranocerta
events.text: A small Roman army routed Tigranes' host, c. site.

events.name: Battle of Zela
events.text: Mithridates destroyed the army of Lucullus' legate Triarius.

steps.label: 66 to 65 BC
steps.title: Pompey takes command
steps.text: Fresh from clearing the Mediterranean of pirates, Pompey received the eastern command. He caught Mithridates at night near the Lycus river and destroyed his army. Tigranes surrendered at Artaxata and became a Roman client, while Mithridates escaped through Colchis and around the Black Sea to Crimea.

events.name: Battle of the Lycus
events.text: Pompey's night attack destroyed Mithridates' last field army.

events.name: Tigranes submits
events.text: Armenia became a Roman client kingdom.

steps.label: 64 to 63 BC
steps.title: Death of Mithridates
steps.text: Mithridates planned to invade Italy from the north, but his son Pharnaces led a revolt, and the old king took his own life at Panticapaeum in 63 BC. Pompey annexed Pontus with Bithynia, made Syria a province, took Jerusalem, and ringed the new provinces with client kings.

events.name: Death of Mithridates
events.text: Abandoned by his army and his son, Mithridates took his own life.

events.name: Pompey takes Jerusalem
events.text: Judea became a Roman client state.

name: Caesar's Gallic Wars
summary: Julius Caesar, governor of Rome's provinces on both sides of the Alps, used a migration of the Helvetii as a pretext to conquer all of independent Gaul. In eight years of campaigns he beat the Gallic and Belgic tribes one by one, crossed the Rhine and the Channel, and crushed the great revolt of Vercingetorix at Alesia in 52 BC. The conquest made Gaul Roman and gave Caesar the army and fortune that carried him to power in Rome.

steps.label: 58 BC
steps.title: Helvetii and Ariovistus
steps.text: The Helvetii set out from the Swiss plateau to settle in western Gaul. Caesar followed them across the Saone and destroyed them near Bibracte, sending the survivors home. That same summer he marched north against the Germanic king Ariovistus, who had settled in Gaul, and drove him back over the Rhine.

events.name: Battle of Bibracte
events.text: Caesar defeated the migrating Helvetii and sent them home.

events.name: Battle against Ariovistus
events.text: The Suebi were routed in Alsace and fled across the Rhine.

steps.label: 57 BC
steps.title: The Belgae
steps.text: Alarmed by the Roman army wintering in their lands, the Belgic tribes of the north gathered a great coalition. Caesar held the line of the Aisne until it broke up, then was nearly overwhelmed by a surprise attack of the Nervii on the Sambre before rallying his legions to win. Publius Crassus meanwhile received the submission of the tribes of Armorica.

moves.label: March to the Aisne and the Sambre

events.name: Battle of the Axona
events.text: The Belgic coalition failed to cross the Aisne and dispersed.

events.name: Battle of the Sabis
events.text: Caesar survived the Nervii's ambush and annihilated them.

steps.label: 56 to 54 BC
steps.title: To the Ocean, the Rhine and Britain
steps.text: Caesar's fleet under Decimus Brutus destroyed the sailing ships of the Veneti off Brittany. In 55 BC Caesar bridged the Rhine in ten days to overawe the Germans, and that summer and the next he crossed to Britain, where he beat the war leader Cassivellaunus north of the Thames before returning to Gaul.

events.name: Battle of Morbihan
events.text: Roman galleys cut the Veneti ships' rigging and destroyed their fleet.

events.name: Bridge over the Rhine
events.text: Caesar's engineers bridged the river to show Rome's reach.

events.name: Cassivellaunus submits
events.text: The British war leader yielded hostages and tribute.

steps.label: 54 to 53 BC
steps.title: Ambiorix
steps.text: In the winter of 54 BC Ambiorix of the Eburones lured fifteen Roman cohorts out of their camp at Atuatuca and massacred them. The Nervii then besieged Quintus Cicero's camp, until Caesar marched to his rescue. In 53 BC Caesar ravaged the land of the Eburones, but Ambiorix was never caught.

events.name: Ambush at Atuatuca
events.text: Sabinus and Cotta and their men were wiped out on the march, c. site.

events.name: Relief of Cicero's camp
events.text: Caesar broke the siege with a small relief army, c. site.

steps.label: 52 BC
steps.title: Vercingetorix and Alesia
steps.text: Vercingetorix of the Arverni united most of Gaul in revolt and fought a scorched earth war. Caesar stormed Avaricum but was thrown back at Gergovia. When Vercingetorix shut himself up in Alesia, Caesar ringed it with two lines of walls, one facing in and one out, beat off a huge Gallic relief army, and forced Vercingetorix to surrender.

events.name: Siege of Avaricum
events.text: Caesar stormed the town and killed almost all its people.

events.name: Battle of Gergovia
events.text: Caesar's only major defeat in Gaul.

events.name: Siege of Alesia
events.text: Vercingetorix surrendered after the relief army failed.

steps.label: 51 to 50 BC
steps.title: Uxellodunum
steps.text: Scattered resistance went on after Alesia. Caesar's last great siege was at Uxellodunum, where he cut off the spring that watered the town and cut off the hands of its captured defenders as a warning. By 50 BC Gaul was pacified, and the next year Caesar crossed the Rubicon with his veteran legions.

events.name: Siege of Uxellodunum
events.text: The last major Gallic stronghold fell when its water was cut off.

name: Roman conquest of Britain
summary: In AD 43 the emperor Claudius sent four legions to conquer Britain. Over forty years Rome overran the southern tribes, hunted down Caratacus, survived the revolt of Boudica, which burned three Roman towns, and pushed into Wales, the north and Scotland. Agricola's victory at Mons Graupius in 83 marked the high point, but Rome never held the far north, which Hadrian later walled off.

steps.label: 43 to 47
steps.title: The Claudian invasion
steps.text: Aulus Plautius landed at Richborough with four legions, beat the British under Caratacus and Togodumnus in a two day battle on the Medway and forced the Thames. The emperor Claudius came in person with elephants to receive the surrender of Camulodunum, while the future emperor Vespasian took the hill forts of the southwest.

events.name: Battle of the Medway
events.text: The British were driven from the river after two days of fighting.

events.name: Surrender of Camulodunum
events.text: Claudius accepted the submission of eleven kings.

events.name: Storming of Maiden Castle
events.text: Vespasian's legion took the great hill fort, c. 44.

steps.label: 47 to 51
steps.title: Caratacus
steps.text: The governor Ostorius Scapula held a frontier along the Fosse Way and turned on the tribes of Wales, where Caratacus led the Silures and Ordovices. Caratacus was defeated in a hill battle in about 50 and fled to the Brigantes, whose queen Cartimandua handed him over in chains. Claudius spared him in Rome.

events.name: Defeat of Caratacus
events.text: Roman legions stormed his hill position on the Welsh border, c. site.

events.name: Cartimandua hands over Caratacus
events.text: The Brigantian queen surrendered the fugitive to Rome.

steps.label: 60 to 61
steps.title: Boudica's revolt
steps.text: While the governor Suetonius Paulinus attacked the druid stronghold of Anglesey, Boudica, queen of the Iceni, rose after Roman officials flogged her and seized her kingdom. Her army burned Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium and cut up the Ninth Legion. Paulinus marched back and, though heavily outnumbered, destroyed her army somewhere along Watling Street.

events.name: Attack on Anglesey
events.text: Paulinus crossed the Menai Strait and destroyed the druids' sanctuary.

events.name: Sack of Londinium
events.text: Boudica's army burned the town and killed its inhabitants.

events.name: Battle of Watling Street
events.text: Paulinus' two legions crushed Boudica's host, c. site.

steps.label: 71 to 78
steps.title: Brigantes and Wales
steps.text: When the Brigantian king Venutius overthrew Cartimandua, Vespasian's governors went on the offensive. Petillius Cerialis conquered the Brigantes of the north, Frontinus subdued the Silures of south Wales, and in 77 to 78 Agricola crushed the Ordovices and took Anglesey.

events.name: Fall of Stanwick
events.text: The great Brigantian stronghold of Venutius fell, c. 72.

steps.label: 79 to 84
steps.title: Mons Graupius
steps.text: Agricola advanced into Scotland, built a line of forts between the Forth and the Clyde and sent his fleet around the north of Britain. In 83 he brought the Caledonians under Calgacus to battle at Mons Graupius and routed them. He was recalled soon after, and Rome pulled back toward the Tyne and Solway, where Hadrian built his wall.

events.name: Battle of Mons Graupius
events.text: Agricola's auxiliaries routed the Caledonians in the far north, c. site.

name: Jewish-Roman Wars
summary: Three great Jewish revolts against Roman rule shook the eastern empire. The First Revolt ended with the destruction of Jerusalem and the Second Temple in 70 and the fall of Masada, a diaspora uprising in Egypt, Cyrene, Cyprus and Mesopotamia was crushed in 115 to 117, and Bar Kokhba's revolt of 132 to 135 ended with Judea devastated and Jews barred from Jerusalem. The wars ended the Temple cult and shifted Jewish life to rabbinic Judaism and the diaspora.

steps.title: The revolt breaks out
steps.text: After years of tension, the procurator Florus seized money from the Temple treasury and Jerusalem rose. Rebels took the city and the fortress of Masada and stopped the sacrifices for the emperor. The governor of Syria, Cestius Gallus, marched on Jerusalem with a legion, then withdrew and was ambushed in the pass of Beth Horon.

events.name: Battle of Beth Horon
events.text: The retreating Roman column lost its baggage and thousands of men.

steps.label: 67 to 69
steps.title: Vespasian takes Galilee
steps.text: Nero sent Vespasian with his son Titus and three legions. They advanced from Ptolemais and took Galilee town by town, including Jotapata, where the rebel commander Josephus surrendered, and Gamla. By 68 the rebels held little more than Jerusalem, Masada and a few desert forts, while inside Jerusalem the factions of John of Gischala and Simon bar Giora fought each other. In 69 Vespasian left to become emperor.

events.name: Siege of Jotapata
events.text: After 47 days the town fell and Josephus went over to Rome.

events.name: Siege of Gamla
events.text: The hilltop town on the Golan was stormed and its people killed.

steps.title: Siege of Jerusalem
steps.text: Titus marched on Jerusalem with four legions in the spring of 70 and broke through its walls one by one. He sealed the city with a siege wall and starved it. In August the Temple was burned and destroyed, and by September the whole city had fallen. Its treasures were carried in triumph through Rome.

events.name: Siege of Jerusalem
events.text: Five months of siege ended with the city in ruins.

events.name: Destruction of the Second Temple
events.text: The Temple burned, ending the sacrificial cult of Judaism.

steps.label: 71 to 74
steps.title: Masada
steps.text: Roman forces reduced the last rebel forts, Herodium and Machaerus. The governor Flavius Silva then besieged Masada, on its desert rock above the Dead Sea, and built a great ramp up to its walls. According to Josephus, the defenders under Eleazar ben Yair killed themselves rather than be taken.

events.name: Siege of Masada
events.text: The last rebel fortress fell in 73 or 74.

steps.label: 115 to 117
steps.title: The diaspora revolt
steps.text: While Trajan campaigned against Parthia, Jewish communities rose in Cyrenaica under Lukuas, in Egypt, on Cyprus and in newly conquered Mesopotamia. The fighting was savage on both sides. Marcius Turbo crushed the revolt in Egypt and Cyrene, and Lusius Quietus put it down in Mesopotamia and then governed Judea.

events.name: Revolt in Cyrene
events.text: Jewish rebels destroyed temples and public buildings.

events.name: Revolt on Cyprus
events.text: Rebels under Artemion devastated Salamis.

events.name: Quietus retakes Edessa and Nisibis
events.text: Mesopotamia was brought back under Roman control.

steps.label: 132 to 133
steps.title: Bar Kokhba
steps.text: Hadrian's plan to rebuild Jerusalem as a Roman colony, Aelia Capitolina, sparked a new revolt led by Simon bar Kosiba, hailed as Bar Kokhba, son of the star. His well prepared rebels, fighting from hidden tunnels and hill villages, drove the Romans out of much of Judea and struck their own coins counting the years of Israel's redemption.

events.name: Revolt of Bar Kokhba
events.text: The rebels set up an independent state in the Judean hills.

steps.label: 134 to 136
steps.title: Betar
steps.text: Hadrian brought his best general, Julius Severus, from Britain with many legions. Severus avoided pitched battle and took the rebel strongholds one by one, starving them out. Betar fell in 135 and Bar Kokhba was killed. Judea was devastated, renamed Syria Palaestina, and Jews were barred from Jerusalem.

events.name: Siege of Betar
events.text: Bar Kokhba's last fortress fell and he was killed.

events.name: Syria Palaestina
events.text: Judea lost its name and Jerusalem became the Roman colony Aelia Capitolina.
